successCriteria: I can describe the trait, psychodynamic, humanistic and social-cognitive approaches to personality

body.hook: Are you more outgoing or reserved? Organized or spontaneous? Psychologists have argued for over a century about what personality is, where it comes from and whether it can change.

vocabulary.definition: A person's consistent patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving.
A stable characteristic, such as being organized or outgoing.
The five broad traits: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (OCEAN).
Freud's approach focusing on unconscious drives and early experiences.
An approach focusing on free will and personal growth, from Maslow and Rogers.
Whether a test gives consistent results.

study.title: Who Are You?
study.question: How do different theories explain personality?
study.passage:
Four approaches:
• Psychodynamic (Sigmund Freud): personality shaped by unconscious conflict between the id (desires), ego (reality) and superego (conscience), and by early childhood. Influential but hard to test scientifically.
• Humanistic (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers): people are basically good and strive for self-actualization; personality grows with acceptance and a healthy self-concept.
• Trait (Big Five, OCEAN): Openness (curious vs traditional), Conscientiousness (organized vs careless), Extraversion (outgoing vs reserved), Agreeableness (cooperative vs competitive), Neuroticism (anxious vs calm). Supported by much research across cultures; traits are partly heritable and fairly stable but can shift with age.
• Social-cognitive (Albert Bandura): personality comes from interaction of thoughts, behaviour and environment; self-efficacy (belief in your ability) matters.
Test check: Many online "personality quizzes" are not reliable or valid. Some, like popular four-letter type tests, have weaker scientific support than the Big Five.
Task: Take a short Big Five inventory (teacher-provided). Then explain one behaviour of a fictional character using all four approaches.
